intro: China is a huge country with 56 officially recognized ethnic groups and many regional languages. Its martial arts grew the same way: as many styles, kept by families, villages, temples, armies and clubs. A Ming general listed many boxing styles around 1560. A national survey in the 1980s recorded well over a hundred.

In this unit you will meet real places and records: the Shaolin Monastery in Henan, the Chen family village, the Jingwu Association of 1910 and the Central Guoshu Institute of 1928. You will see how the People's Republic turned martial arts into wushu, a sport with two codes, taolu and sanda. Then you will follow Chinese arts onto film screens in Hong Kong and the United States.

By the end, you will be able to tell a legend from a record and a film name from a school name. You will be able to name a style by its place, its lineage and its governing body, instead of one English word.
bigQuestion: Why is it more accurate to speak of many Chinese martial arts than of one thing called kung fu?

title: China Is Not One Kung Fu

chapters.title: Many Systems
chapters.bigQuestion: Why do historians say China has many martial arts, not one called kung fu?

story.title: One Building, Two Plans
story.kicker: A floor plan for a form and a ring plan for a sport hang in the same sports hall.
paragraphs: A sports hall in a Chinese city has two notices taped by its door. The first is a floor plan for a wushu routine. It shows a large rectangle of carpet where one athlete performs alone. A row of judges' tables sits along one side, facing the carpet.

The second notice is a ring plan for sanda. It shows a raised square platform with padded edges. Two athletes will meet there in timed rounds, with a referee between them. The two plans belong to two different competitions under one governing body.

A visiting student reads both notices and frowns. At home, she has only heard one English name for all of this: kung fu. The names on these plans are different. One says taolu. The other says sanda. Neither says kung fu.

Behind the two notices lie many centuries of history. China has village styles, family styles and temple stories. It had a national program in the 1920s and 1930s. Since the 1950s it has had state sport rules. Each layer gave the arts new names, new rooms and new rule books.
story.think: Why might one building need two different plans for two events that share a Chinese name?

lessons.title: One Country, Many Arts
lessons.mainIdea: China is a huge country with many peoples, and its fighting arts grew as many separate styles, not as one system.
reading: China today covers about 9.6 million square kilometers. That is close to the size of the United States. The People's Republic of China officially recognizes 56 ethnic groups. The Han are the largest. Hui, Mongol, Manchu, Tibetan and many other peoples also live there. Regions differ in language, food and custom, and their fighting arts differ too.

A Ming dynasty general named Qi Jiguang (1528–1588) trained soldiers to fight coastal pirates. Around 1560 he wrote a military manual called the Jixiao Xinshu. One chapter covers unarmed boxing. In it, Qi listed many boxing styles known in his day. Each named *style* had its own teachers. Even 450 years ago, a writer saw many arts, not one.

Chinese arts also include more than boxing. The old Chinese wrestling tradition is called *shuaijiao*. The Qing court, ruled by Manchu emperors from 1644 to 1912, kept a corps of palace wrestlers. Mongolian wrestling is its own tradition. It is still the center of the Naadam festival each July in Mongolia.

Some styles grew inside particular communities. Hui Muslims are a Chinese-speaking Muslim people. Hui communities in northern China have long been linked with styles such as Chaquan. Cangzhou, a city in Hebei province, is famous for its many martial arts schools. A map of China's arts looks like a map of its peoples and places.

words.d: one named martial art system with its own teachers, forms and history
an old Chinese wrestling tradition, practiced at the Qing court and still competed today
a Chinese-speaking Muslim people who live in many parts of China

look.title: A General Lists the Boxers
look.text: In his boxing chapter, Qi Jiguang names several boxing styles of his time and the families or teachers linked to them. He says each has its strong points, and he chooses what he thinks will help soldiers.
look.cite: Qi Jiguang, Jixiao Xinshu (New Treatise on Military Efficiency), c. 1560, boxing chapter
look.prompt: What does Qi's list tell us about how many boxing styles existed in Ming China?

check.q: How many ethnic groups does the People's Republic of China officially recognize?
check.why: China officially recognizes 56 ethnic groups; the Han are the largest.

check.q: Who wrote the Jixiao Xinshu around 1560?
check.why: The Ming general Qi Jiguang wrote this military manual, which lists many boxing styles.

check.q: What is shuaijiao?
check.why: Shuaijiao is Chinese wrestling; the Qing court kept palace wrestlers.

lessons.title: North and South
lessons.mainIdea: People often sort Chinese styles into northern and southern families, but that is a rough grouping, not a strict rule.
reading: The Yangtze River crosses China from west to east. Many people use it as a rough line between north and south. Martial arts writers often sort styles into *northern* and *southern* families using that line. The grouping is old and popular. Historians treat it as a loose label, because teachers moved and styles mixed.

Northern families include Changquan, which means long fist, and Baji, linked to Cangzhou in Hebei. Taijiquan, Xingyiquan and Baguazhang also took shape in the north. Baguazhang is traced to Dong Haichuan, a teacher in Beijing in the 1800s.

Southern families grew strong in Guangdong and Fujian provinces. Hung Gar, Choy Li Fut and Wing Chun come from Guangdong. White Crane styles come from Fujian. Many southern teachers later moved to Hong Kong. From there, and with emigrants, these styles reached Southeast Asia and North America.

A popular saying compares the two regions in a single short phrase. Like most sayings, it hides many exceptions. A *generalization* is a statement that is true of many cases but not all. The north and south labels help readers find a style on the map. They cannot tell a reader everything about that style.

words.d: a label for Chinese styles that grew mostly north of the Yangtze River
a label for Chinese styles that grew mostly in the south, such as Guangdong and Fujian
a statement that is true of many cases but not every case

look.title: Two Pins on a Map
look.text: A teacher puts two pins on a wall map of China. One pin is on Beijing, where Baguazhang was taught in the 1800s. The other is on Foshan in Guangdong, a home of Wing Chun and Hung Gar teachers. A thin blue line, the Yangtze River, runs between the pins.
look.prompt: Which pin marks a northern style and which marks a southern one? Why is the river only a rough guide?

check.q: Which river is often used as a rough line between northern and southern China?
check.why: The Yangtze crosses China west to east and is a common north–south dividing line.

check.q: Which province is home to Hung Gar, Choy Li Fut and Wing Chun?
check.why: These three southern styles come from Guangdong.

check.q: Why do historians call the north–south split a generalization?
choices: Because teachers moved and styles mixed
Because no styles exist in the south
Because the government banned the words
Because it only applies to wrestling
check.why: The label is true of many styles but not all, since teachers traveled and borrowed.

lessons.title: Family and Village Styles
lessons.mainIdea: Many Chinese styles were kept by families and villages; taijiquan grew from the Chen family village and branched into several family lines.
reading: Chenjiagou is a village in Wen County, Henan province. Its name means Chen family ditch. The Chen family practiced a martial art there that became known as taijiquan. For generations, the art passed mostly inside the family. A family style like this is passed on through a *lineage*, a line of teachers and students.

In the early 1800s, a man named Yang Luchan (1799–1872) learned the art in Chenjiagou. He was not a member of the Chen family. He later taught in Beijing, including to members of the Qing elite. His version became known as Yang style. His sons and grandsons carried it on.

More family lines grew from these two. Historians usually name five main family styles of taijiquan: Chen, Yang, Wu (Wu Jianquan's line), Wu or Hao (Wu Yuxiang's line) and Sun. Each carries a family name. Each keeps its own history of teachers.

Taijiquan is now practiced by millions of people, often for health. In 2020, UNESCO added taijiquan to its list of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity. The term *intangible heritage* means living customs, skills and knowledge, not buildings. The listing named China as the home of the practice.

words.d: a line of teachers and students who pass an art down over generations
a Chinese martial art that grew from the Chen family village in Henan; often called tai chi in English
living customs, skills and knowledge that a community keeps, as opposed to buildings or objects

look.title: Five Names on a Poster
look.text: A community center in Chicago posts a list of classes: Chen style taijiquan on Monday, Yang style on Wednesday, Sun style on Saturday. All three are listed under the same heading, Tai Chi. Each teacher's biography names a different line of teachers.
look.prompt: What do the family names on the poster tell you that the single heading Tai Chi does not?

check.why: Chenjiagou is in Wen County, Henan.

check.q: Who carried the art from Chenjiagou and taught it in Beijing in the 1800s?
check.why: Yang Luchan, not a Chen family member, learned in Chenjiagou and taught in Beijing.

check.q: What did UNESCO do with taijiquan in 2020?
choices: Added it to its list of Intangible Cultural Heritage
Named it the national sport of Japan
check.why: UNESCO listed taijiquan as Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in 2020.

lessons.title: The Shaolin Monastery
lessons.mainIdea: Shaolin is a real Buddhist monastery in Henan whose monks are documented as fighters in some periods of Chinese history.
reading: The Shaolin Monastery stands on Mount Song, near the city of Dengfeng in Henan province. It is a Buddhist *monastery*, a home for monks. Chinese records say it was founded in 495 CE. A Northern Wei emperor built it for an Indian monk named Batuo.

Some Shaolin history is carved in stone. A *stele* is an upright stone slab with writing on it. A stele at Shaolin, dated 728, records that monks helped Li Shimin around 621. Li Shimin later became Emperor Taizong of the Tang dynasty. The monastery received land as a reward.

In the 1550s, during the Ming dynasty, Shaolin monks joined government campaigns against pirates on China's east coast. Ming writers recorded their service. The historian Meir Shahar gathered these records in his 2008 book The Shaolin Monastery. He shows that monks fought for rulers as early as the Tang, and that Shaolin's own fighting methods are well documented from the Ming period on.

Today Shaolin is both a working monastery and a famous place for visitors. In 2010, UNESCO listed it as part of the Historic Monuments of Dengfeng, a World Heritage site. Many schools near the monastery now teach martial arts to thousands of students.

words.d: a place where monks live, study and practice their religion
an upright stone slab carved with writing, often to record an event
a Buddhist monastery on Mount Song in Henan, China, founded in 495 CE

look.title: Shaolin Through the Centuries
rows: Named part of a World Heritage site
look.cite: Shaolin stele of 728; Meir Shahar, The Shaolin Monastery (2008); UNESCO World Heritage List
look.prompt: About how many years passed between the monks' help to Li Shimin and the stele that recorded it?

check.q: In which province is the Shaolin Monastery?
check.why: Shaolin stands on Mount Song near Dengfeng, Henan.

check.q: What is a stele?
choices: An upright stone slab carved with writing
check.why: A stele is a carved stone slab; Shaolin's stele of 728 records the monks' help to Li Shimin.

check.q: Which book gathered records of Shaolin monks as fighters?
check.why: Shahar's 2008 book collects Tang and Ming records about Shaolin.

lessons.title: Bodhidharma: Legend and Record
lessons.mainIdea: A popular legend says the monk Bodhidharma created Shaolin fighting, but historians trace that story to texts written about a thousand years after him.
reading: Bodhidharma was a Buddhist monk from India or Central Asia. Chan Buddhist tradition says he came to China around 500 CE. Chan tradition also says he meditated in a cave near Shaolin for nine years. He is honored as the first teacher of Chan, the school called Zen in Japan.

A later *legend* says Bodhidharma taught the monks exercises that became Shaolin fighting. This story is often told in martial arts schools around the world. Early records of Bodhidharma, however, say nothing about fighting. The oldest texts about him focus on meditation and teaching.

The legend is tied to a book called the Yijin Jing, or Sinew-Changing Classic. The book claims Bodhidharma as its author. Historians date it to the 1600s, more than a thousand years after he lived. In the 1930s, the Chinese historian Tang Hao studied these texts. He argued that the link to Bodhidharma was added much later.

Historians do not call the legend worthless. A legend shows what people valued and how they explained their art. A *historical record* is a document from the time that can be checked. Both matter, but they answer different questions.

words.d: a traditional story about the past that may not be supported by records
a document from the time, such as a letter, stele or official report, that historians can check
a Buddhist monk honored in Chan and Zen tradition as a founding teacher; legend links him to Shaolin fighting

look.title: Two Signs at One Gate
look.text: Sign A, at a school gate: 'Our art began when Bodhidharma taught the Shaolin monks.' Sign B, in a museum case: 'The earliest records of Shaolin monks fighting date from the Tang dynasty; the Bodhidharma story appears in a book from the 1600s.'
look.prompt: Which sign reports a legend and which reports historical records? How could both be useful to a historian?

check.q: What do the oldest texts about Bodhidharma focus on?
check.why: Early records describe Bodhidharma as a meditation teacher, not a fighter.

check.q: When do historians date the Yijin Jing?
check.why: The Yijin Jing dates to the 1600s, long after Bodhidharma lived.

check.q: What did the historian Tang Hao argue in the 1930s?
choices: The link to Bodhidharma was added much later
check.why: Tang Hao studied the texts and found the Bodhidharma link was a later addition.

lessons.title: Shaolin and Wudang
lessons.mainIdea: Writers from 1669 on split Chinese arts into external and internal families linked to Shaolin and Wudang, a grouping that mixes history and legend.
reading: The Wudang Mountains are in Hubei province. They hold many Daoist temples and palaces. *Daoism* is a Chinese tradition of religion and thought. In 1994, UNESCO listed the ancient buildings of Wudang as a World Heritage site.

In 1669, the scholar Huang Zongxi wrote an epitaph for a boxer named Wang Zhengnan. An epitaph is writing in honor of someone who has died. In it, Huang contrasted an *external* school, linked with Shaolin, and an *internal* school. He traced the internal school to Zhang Sanfeng, a Daoist of Wudang.

Zhang Sanfeng appears in many stories, but historians cannot confirm the details of his life. The idea that he invented taijiquan is a legend. It spread widely in the late 1800s and early 1900s. Taijiquan's documented history starts with the Chen family village, not with Wudang.

The internal and external labels are still used today. Taijiquan, Xingyiquan and Baguazhang are often grouped as internal arts. Historians treat the grouping as a way people organized the arts. It is not proof of where each art began.

words.d: a Chinese tradition of religion and thought; the Wudang Mountains hold many Daoist temples
a label first used by writers in the 1600s for arts linked to Wudang, such as taijiquan
a label for arts linked to Shaolin, set against the internal arts
writing in honor of a person who has died

look.title: An Epitaph for a Boxer
look.text: Huang Zongxi writes that Shaolin boxing is famous, but that there is another school he calls internal. He says this internal school traces back to Zhang Sanfeng of Wudang, and that Wang Zhengnan was one of its masters.
look.cite: Huang Zongxi, Epitaph for Wang Zhengnan, 1669
look.prompt: Which two schools does Huang compare? Why might a historian be careful about his claim about Zhang Sanfeng?

check.q: In which province are the Wudang Mountains?
check.why: The Wudang Mountains, with their Daoist temples, are in Hubei.

check.q: Who first wrote about an internal school set against Shaolin, in 1669?
check.why: Huang Zongxi's epitaph for Wang Zhengnan contrasts internal and external schools.

check.q: What do historians say about Zhang Sanfeng inventing taijiquan?
choices: It is proven by a Tang stele
It is recorded in the Olympic charter
It is a legend that cannot be confirmed
check.why: Taijiquan's documented history begins with the Chen village; the Zhang Sanfeng story is a legend.

lessons.title: Boxers and the Jingwu Association
lessons.mainIdea: After the Boxer Uprising of 1899–1901, reformers such as the Jingwu Athletic Association of 1910 recast martial arts as modern physical education.
reading: In 1899, a movement grew in northern China that foreign writers called the Boxers. Its members belonged to groups that practiced martial arts and rituals. They attacked foreign missionaries, Chinese Christians and foreign property. In 1900, they laid siege to the foreign legations in Beijing.

An army from eight foreign nations, called the Eight-Nation Alliance, crushed the *Boxer Uprising*. The Qing government signed the Boxer Protocol in 1901. It had to pay huge sums to the foreign powers. Afterward, many Chinese reformers wanted martial arts linked with science and school, not with rebellion.

The Jingwu Athletic Association opened in Shanghai in 1910. Its name is often written Chin Woo, from the Cantonese. It is linked to the well-known fighter Huo Yuanjia, who died that same year. Jingwu taught several styles side by side, instead of one family art. It also offered other sports, music and lectures.

Jingwu was an *association*, a club with members, officers and written rules. It opened branches in other Chinese cities. In the 1920s it spread to Southeast Asia, including Singapore and Malaya. Chinese communities there kept Jingwu clubs running for many decades.

words.d: an anti-foreign movement in northern China from 1899 to 1901, crushed by an eight-nation army
a club with members, officers and written rules
the Jingwu (Chin Woo) Athletic Association, founded in Shanghai in 1910

look.title: Two Kinds of Membership
look.text: Picture two scenes. In 1899, a village group practices boxing and rituals in a temple yard. In 1915, a Shanghai club keeps a printed list of members, holds classes in several styles and runs a photography club. Both groups practice martial arts.
look.prompt: How did the Jingwu club change the setting in which martial arts were taught?

check.q: When did the Boxer Uprising take place?
check.why: The Boxer Uprising ran from 1899 to 1901 and ended with the Boxer Protocol.

check.q: Where and when was the Jingwu Athletic Association founded?
check.why: Jingwu opened in Shanghai in 1910.

check.q: How was Jingwu different from a family style?
choices: It taught only one secret art
It refused to keep written rules
It taught several styles side by side
check.why: Jingwu offered several styles plus other sports and lectures, as a modern association.

lessons.title: Guoshu: The National Art
lessons.mainIdea: In 1928 the Republic of China founded the Central Guoshu Institute to turn many styles into one national program.
reading: The Republic of China replaced the Qing dynasty in 1912. In 1928, the Nationalist government set up its capital in Nanjing. That year it founded the Central Guoshu Institute there. The word *guoshu* means national art. The name told people that martial arts belonged to the whole nation, not only to families or villages.

The institute was led by Zhang Zhijiang, a Nationalist general. It trained teachers and published books. It set up branch institutes in provinces and counties. It held national examinations in 1928 and 1933, where fighters from many styles competed.

Guoshu leaders wanted martial arts taught in schools and the army. They linked the arts with health and national strength. Many Chinese at the time felt their country had been humiliated by foreign powers. A strong body was presented as a patriotic duty.

In 1936, a Chinese martial arts team gave a *demonstration* at the Berlin Olympic Games. A demonstration is a display, not a medal event. The team showed routines to an international crowd. The war with Japan from 1937 soon disrupted the institute's work.

words.d: national art; the name the Republic of China used for martial arts from 1928
a national martial arts institute founded in Nanjing in 1928 by the Nationalist government
a display of a sport or art at a games, with no medals given

look.title: Building a National Program
look.cite: Andrew D. Morris, Marrow of the Nation: A History of Sport and Physical Culture in Republican China (2004)
look.prompt: How many years did the institute run before the war with Japan disrupted it?

check.q: What does guoshu mean?
check.why: Guoshu means national art, the Republic's name for martial arts.

check.q: Where was the Central Guoshu Institute founded in 1928?
check.why: The Nationalist government founded it in its capital, Nanjing.

check.q: What happened at the 1936 Berlin Olympics?
choices: Sanda had its first world title
A Chinese team gave a martial arts demonstration
check.why: A Chinese team performed a demonstration, not a medal event, in Berlin.

lessons.title: Wushu in the People's Republic
lessons.mainIdea: After 1949 the People's Republic of China turned martial arts into state sport called wushu, with standard routines, then later surveyed older styles.
reading: The People's Republic of China was founded in 1949. The new government chose the word *wushu* for martial arts. Wushu simply means martial art. Many guoshu teachers moved to Taiwan or Hong Kong, where the older name stayed in use.

In 1952, the state created a sports commission to run physical culture and sport. In the 1950s, officials and coaches wrote *standardized* routines. Standardized means made the same everywhere, so that athletes across China could be judged by one set of rules. Wushu joined national sports meetings and school programs.

During the Cultural Revolution, from 1966 to 1976, many traditional teachers were attacked. Old styles were often seen as feudal, or tied to the past. Some teachers stopped teaching in public. Performance wushu for sport and display continued in some places.

In the 1980s, the government sponsored a national survey of traditional styles. Researchers recorded well over a hundred distinct styles and collected old books and interviews. The survey showed again that China's arts are many, not one.

words.d: martial art; the name the People's Republic of China uses for martial arts and for its competitive sport
made the same everywhere so that everyone follows one set of rules
a political campaign in China from 1966 to 1976 that attacked many traditions and teachers

look.title: Two Teachers, One City
look.text: In 1960, two teachers live in the same Chinese city. One coaches a provincial team using a printed routine that every province also uses. The other teaches his grandfather's style to a few neighbors in a courtyard, with no printed book at all.
look.prompt: Which teacher works inside the state sport system? What might each teacher gain or lose?

check.q: What name did the People's Republic of China choose for martial arts?
check.why: The People's Republic used wushu, meaning martial art.

check.q: Why were wushu routines standardized in the 1950s?
choices: So athletes across China could be judged by one set of rules
So every family could keep its own secret form
check.why: Standard routines let judges compare athletes from all over China.

check.q: What did the 1980s national survey find?
choices: Martial arts had come from Japan
Well over a hundred distinct styles
check.why: Researchers recorded well over a hundred styles, showing the arts' variety.

lessons.title: Taolu: A Judged Composition
lessons.mainIdea: Taolu is the wushu event in which judges score a solo routine, much as judges score gymnastics or figure skating.
reading: The word *taolu* means routine or set. In a taolu event, one athlete performs a planned sequence alone on a carpet. Panels of judges watch from tables beside it. They award a score, the way judges score gymnastics or figure skating. Nobody faces an opponent.

The International Wushu Federation, or *IWUF*, was founded in 1990. It held the first World Wushu Championships in Beijing in 1991. The IWUF writes the international rules for taolu. Its judges score the quality of movements, the overall performance and the difficulty.

Taolu events are named for families of routines and for objects carried in them. Changquan is a northern family. Nanquan, meaning southern fist, gathers southern styles into one event. Taijiquan also has its own event. Other events use a broadsword, a straight sword, a staff or a spear. Athletes often train in state sports schools from childhood.

In 2008, Beijing hosted a wushu tournament during the Olympic Games. It was approved by the IOC but was not an official Olympic medal sport. Athletes received medals from the organizers, not official Olympic medals. Wushu leaders have long hoped to reach the Olympic program.

words.d: a wushu event in which one athlete performs a set routine and judges award a score
the International Wushu Federation, founded in 1990, which writes world wushu rules
a group of officials who watch and score a performance together

look.title: Wushu Goes International
rows: Wushu tournament at the Beijing Olympics
look.cite: International Wushu Federation records; UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage lists
look.prompt: How many years after the IWUF was founded did Beijing hold its Olympic wushu tournament?

check.q: What does an athlete do in a taolu event?
choices: Performs a set routine alone for judges
check.why: Taolu is a solo routine scored by judges.

check.q: When was the International Wushu Federation founded?
check.why: The IWUF was founded in 1990 and held its first world championships in 1991.

check.q: What was the status of wushu at the 2008 Beijing Olympics?
choices: A special tournament, not an official medal sport
A demonstration held only for children
check.why: Wushu had an IOC-approved tournament in 2008, but not official Olympic medals.

lessons.title: Sanda: A Ring Code
lessons.mainIdea: Sanda is the wushu event in which two athletes compete on a raised platform under timed rules, a separate code from taolu.
reading: The event called *sanda*, also known as sanshou, is the wushu event in which two athletes face each other. It grew as a state sport in China from the late 1970s and 1980s. Coaches and officials wrote its rules to fit modern sport: weight classes, protective gear, referees and timed rounds.

Sanda matches take place on a raised square *platform*. Chinese history has older stories of fighters meeting on raised stages called leitai. The modern platform borrows that idea. The IWUF now runs world championships in sanda as well as taolu.

Sanda and taolu share a governing body and the name wushu. They are still different codes. A *code* is a full set of rules for one sport. Taolu measures a performance against a standard. Sanda measures one athlete against another, with points and a referee.

Other governing bodies use other rules and names. Kickboxing and mixed martial arts leagues, for example, have their own codes. A sanda title is won under IWUF or national wushu rules, not theirs. Knowing the code tells a reader what a win or a record really means.

words.d: the wushu event in which two athletes compete under timed rules; also called sanshou
the raised square stage on which sanda matches take place
a complete set of rules for one sport or event

check.why: Sanda is also called sanshou.

choices: A complete set of rules for one sport
check.why: A code is a full rule set; taolu and sanda are two different codes.

check.why: Taolu scores a solo performance; sanda sets two athletes against each other.

lessons.title: One English Word for a Map
lessons.mainIdea: The English word kung fu covers many Chinese arts, codes and communities, so careful writers name the style, place and body instead.
reading: In Chinese, *gongfu* means skill gained through long, hard effort. A cook or a calligrapher can have gongfu. The Cantonese form sounds like gung fu. In English, kung fu became a common name for Chinese martial arts in the 1960s and 1970s.

One English word now stands for a huge map. It can mean a Hung Gar school in Hong Kong or a taijiquan class in a park. It can also mean a taolu team in Beijing or a sanda gym. Each has its own teachers, rules and history. Using only one word can *flatten* those differences.

Chinese speakers use many names for these arts. Wushu, guoshu, quanfa and the names of each style are all in use. In Taiwan, Hong Kong and Chinese communities abroad, schools often use the older word guoshu or the style name.

Careful writers name what they mean. They say Wing Chun from Foshan or Chen style taijiquan from Henan. For sport they name the IWUF sanda code. They name the style, the place and the governing body. This habit helps readers respect each community's own history.

words.d: a Chinese word for skill gained through long effort; the source of the English word kung fu
to treat many different things as if they were one, hiding their differences

check.why: Gongfu means skill from effort; a cook can have gongfu too.

check.why: The word spread in English in the 1960s and 1970s.

chapters.title: Name the Room Not the Movie
chapters.bigQuestion: How did films change the names people use for Chinese martial arts, and how can we find the real schools behind them?

story.title: A Poster and a Charter
story.kicker: A movie poster and a school charter use the same word in two very different ways.
paragraphs: Two pieces of paper hang in the front window of a small school near Chinatown in Chicago. One is an old movie poster. It shows a hero leaping over a temple roof, with red letters that promise ancient secrets. The word kung fu runs across the top in huge type.

The other paper is the school's charter, framed behind glass. It gives the name of the style the school teaches. It names the city in Guangdong where the style's teachers came from. It lists the school's teachers, one after another, for four generations. It gives the year the school opened.

A visitor notices that the two papers disagree. The poster uses kung fu to mean magic and mystery. The charter never uses the word at all. It names one style, one place and one line of real people, each with a name and a date.

Both papers tell a kind of history. The poster tells the history of films, studios and audiences. The charter tells the history of a school, a family of teachers and a community that moved across an ocean. A careful reader learns to tell them apart.
story.think: What can the charter tell you that the poster cannot? What can the poster tell you about its own time?

lessons.title: Spelling a Chinese Word
lessons.mainIdea: Chinese words are spelled in English letters by different systems, so one art can have several English spellings.
reading: Chinese is written in characters, not in an alphabet. To write Chinese words in English letters, people use a *romanization* system. In the 1800s, two British scholars, Thomas Wade and Herbert Giles, built one system. It is called Wade–Giles, and it gave English the spelling kung fu.

In 1958, the People's Republic of China adopted a new system called *pinyin*. In pinyin, the same word is spelled gongfu. Taiji replaced t'ai chi, and Beijing replaced Peking. In 1982, the International Organization for Standardization approved pinyin as a world standard.

Spelling also depends on the spoken language. Mandarin is the national language of China. Cantonese is spoken in Guangdong and Hong Kong. Many teachers who brought southern styles abroad spoke Cantonese. That is why English uses Cantonese forms such as Wing Chun and Hung Gar.

So one art may appear with several spellings on signs and in books. A reader who knows the systems can see that tai chi and taiji name the same art. Spelling changes do not make a new style. They show which language and which decade a writer came from.

words.d: a system for writing words from another script in English (Roman) letters
the romanization system adopted by the People's Republic of China in 1958
a Chinese language spoken in Guangdong and Hong Kong

look.title: Three Signs, One Art
look.text: Three signs hang in three cities. The first, from the 1970s, says T'ai Chi Ch'uan. The second, from the 2010s, says Taijiquan. The third, a park flyer, says simply Tai Chi. All three advertise classes in the same family style.
look.prompt: Which spelling system did each sign use? Why might the older sign use a different spelling?

check.q: Which romanization system gave English the spelling kung fu?
check.why: Wade–Giles, built by Thomas Wade and Herbert Giles, spells the word kung fu.

check.q: When did the People's Republic of China adopt pinyin?
check.why: China adopted pinyin in 1958; it became an international standard in 1982.

check.q: Why are Wing Chun and Hung Gar spelled in Cantonese forms?
choices: Their teachers abroad often spoke Cantonese
Pinyin has no letters for them
They were named by a film studio
check.why: Many southern teachers came from Cantonese-speaking Guangdong and Hong Kong.

lessons.title: Schools in Chinese America
lessons.mainIdea: United States immigration laws shaped when Chinese teachers could arrive, and schools grew inside Chinatown communities before opening widely.
reading: In 1882, Congress passed the *Chinese Exclusion Act*. It stopped Chinese laborers from coming to the United States. It was the first major U.S. law to shut out people of one nationality. Congress repealed it in 1943, during World War II, but kept a tiny yearly quota.

Chinese Americans built their own institutions under these limits. They formed family associations, merchant associations and benevolent societies. In Chicago, Chinatown grew around Cermak Road and Wentworth Avenue from about 1912. The On Leong Merchants Association building there opened in the late 1920s. It is now the Pui Tak Center.

Martial arts often lived inside these community groups. Many lion dance teams trained with a martial arts teacher. They performed at Lunar New Year and at openings of businesses. Classes were often taught in Cantonese to members of the community.

The Immigration and Nationality Act of 1965 ended the old national quotas. Many more Chinese immigrants arrived, including teachers. At the same time, more schools began teaching students from outside Chinatown. By the 1970s, Chinese martial arts schools had opened in cities across the country.

words.d: an 1882 U.S. law that stopped Chinese laborers from immigrating; repealed in 1943
a community group that helps its members with needs such as jobs, housing and funerals
a U.S. law that ended the old national quotas and opened immigration more widely

look.title: An 1882 Law
look.text: The act suspended the coming of Chinese laborers to the United States for ten years. It also said that no state or federal court could admit Chinese people to citizenship.
look.cite: Chinese Exclusion Act, May 6, 1882 (47th U.S. Congress)
look.prompt: How might this law have affected the number of Chinese martial arts teachers in the United States before 1943?

check.q: What did the Chinese Exclusion Act of 1882 do?
choices: It stopped Chinese laborers from immigrating
It made kung fu a school subject
check.why: The 1882 act shut out Chinese laborers and was not repealed until 1943.

check.q: Where did Chicago's Chinatown grow from about 1912?

check.why: The Immigration and Nationality Act of 1965 opened immigration more widely.

lessons.title: Hong Kong Studios
lessons.mainIdea: Hong Kong film studios built martial arts films into a world genre, using story names that often differ from real school names.
reading: From the 1950s to the 1980s, Hong Kong was a center of Chinese-language filmmaking. The Shaw Brothers studio ran a huge studio lot there called Movietown. Golden Harvest, founded in 1970 by Raymond Chow and Leonard Ho, became its great rival. Both made hundreds of martial arts films.

Filmmakers worked in two main kinds of story. Each kind is a *genre*. The word *wuxia* means martial hero. Wuxia stories are usually set in the distant past and often include swords and flying heroes. Kung fu films, popular from the late 1960s, focused more on unarmed fighters in recent history.

Many films drew on wuxia novels. The writer Jin Yong, whose real name was Louis Cha (1924–2018), published famous wuxia novels in Hong Kong newspapers from 1955 to 1972. His stories include invented sects beside real places such as Shaolin and Wudang. Readers across the Chinese-speaking world knew his invented names.

In 2000, Ang Lee's film Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon brought wuxia to world audiences. It was based on a novel by Wang Dulu. The film won four Academy Awards, including Best Foreign Language Film. Its sword schools and secret manuals come from fiction, not from school records.

words.d: a kind or category of story, film or art
martial hero; a Chinese genre of stories about heroes in the distant past
a company that makes films, often on its own large site

look.title: A Sect on the Page
look.text: A wuxia novel describes a mountain sect with a secret manual, a founder who lived three hundred years ago and a rival sect across a valley. The novel also mentions Shaolin Monastery, a real place in Henan.
look.prompt: Which details might be invented, and which one is real? How could you check?

check.q: What does wuxia mean?
check.why: Wuxia means martial hero, a genre of stories set in the distant past.

check.q: Which studio was founded in 1970 by Raymond Chow and Leonard Ho?
check.why: Golden Harvest was founded in 1970 and became Shaw Brothers' rival.

check.q: Where do the sword schools in Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon come from?
choices: From fiction, based on a novel by Wang Dulu
check.why: The film adapts Wang Dulu's novel; its schools are fictional.

lessons.title: Bruce Lee's Short Career
lessons.mainIdea: Bruce Lee made four finished starring films in three years, and they made the word kung fu famous around the world.
reading: Bruce Lee was born in San Francisco in 1940 and grew up in Hong Kong. He acted in films as a child. In Hong Kong he studied Wing Chun with the teacher Ip Man. In 1959 he moved to the United States. He studied at the University of Washington and began teaching in Seattle.

In 1966 and 1967, Lee played Kato on the American television show The Green Hornet. Then he returned to Hong Kong and signed with Golden Harvest. The Big Boss came out in 1971. Fist of Fury and The Way of the Dragon followed in 1972. Each broke box office records in Hong Kong.

Enter the Dragon was made with the American studio Warner Bros. Lee died in Hong Kong on July 20, 1973, at age 32. The film opened in the United States weeks later. It became a worldwide hit and helped start a kung fu film *craze* in the West.

Lee's fame made the word kung fu known in many languages. His films named some real places and schools and invented others. His *legacy* includes films, a school name he created and his writings, later published by his family and students.

words.d: a sudden, widespread popular interest that often fades later
what a person leaves behind that others remember and use
the money a film earns from ticket sales

look.prompt: How many years passed between Lee's first and last finished starring film?

check.why: Lee studied Wing Chun with Ip Man before moving to the United States in 1959.

check.q: Which film was made with Warner Bros. and released after Lee's death?
check.why: Enter the Dragon opened weeks after Lee died on July 20, 1973.

check.q: What role did Lee play on The Green Hornet in 1966 and 1967?
check.why: Lee played Kato on the American show before his Hong Kong films.

lessons.title: Wong Fei-hung on Screen
lessons.mainIdea: Wong Fei-hung was a real Cantonese healer and teacher who became the hero of more Chinese films than almost anyone.
reading: Wong Fei-hung lived from 1847 to 1925 in Guangdong province. He was a martial arts teacher linked with the Hung Gar style. He also ran a clinic that treated injuries with traditional Chinese medicine. His clinic was known as Po Chi Lam. Records of his daily life are few.

In 1949, a Hong Kong film called The True Story of Wong Fei-hung came out. The actor Kwan Tak-hing played Wong. Kwan went on to play him in dozens of films over the next decades. Few real people have appeared as heroes in so many films.

Later filmmakers kept the name but changed the stories. In Drunken Master (1978), Jackie Chan played a young, mischievous Wong. In Once Upon a Time in China (1991), Jet Li played Wong as a national hero facing foreign powers. Each film reflected its own decade.

A *screen persona* is the character audiences know from films. Wong's screen persona grew far larger than the records of his life. Historians separate the documented teacher and healer from the film hero. The Hung Gar schools that honor him keep their own lineage records.

words.d: the character that audiences know from films, which may differ from the real person
a southern Chinese style from Guangdong, linked with Wong Fei-hung
a long-standing Chinese system of healing that includes herbs and treatment of injuries

look.title: A Life and Its Films
rows: Once Upon a Time in China
look.cite: Wong Fei-hung Memorial Hall, Foshan; Hong Kong Film Archive
look.prompt: How many years after Wong's death did the first film about him appear?

check.q: Besides teaching, what work did Wong Fei-hung do?
choices: He ran a clinic for injuries
check.why: Wong ran the Po Chi Lam clinic using traditional Chinese medicine.

check.q: Which actor played Wong in dozens of films starting in 1949?
check.why: Kwan Tak-hing first played Wong in The True Story of Wong Fei-hung, 1949.

check.q: What is a screen persona?
choices: The character audiences know from films
check.why: Wong's screen persona grew larger than the records of his real life.

lessons.title: Huo Yuanjia and Chen Zhen
lessons.mainIdea: Fist of Fury and Fearless use the real Huo Yuanjia and the real Jingwu Association, but their plots mix history with invention.
reading: Huo Yuanjia was a real fighter from Tianjin who died in 1910. He is linked with the founding of the Jingwu Athletic Association in Shanghai that year. Stories about his challenges to foreign fighters spread widely. Historians note that the details of those stories are hard to confirm.

Bruce Lee's 1972 film Fist of Fury is set at the Jingwu school in Shanghai just after Huo's death. Lee plays Chen Zhen, a student who seeks justice for his teacher. Chen Zhen is a *fictional* character, invented for the screen. Later films and television shows brought him back many times.

In 2006, Jet Li starred as Huo Yuanjia in a film called Fearless. It tells Huo's life as a story of pride, loss and change. The filmmakers invented or reshaped many events for drama. Fifteen years earlier, Jet Li had played Wong Fei-hung in Once Upon a Time in China.

A *historical film* is set in the past but is made to entertain. It may use real names, real places and real dates. It may also add invented people and events. Historians compare such films with records, the way they compare legends with steles.

words.d: invented for a story, not a real person or event
a film set in the past that uses real names and places but may add invented events
a real fighter from Tianjin, died 1910, linked with the founding of the Jingwu Association

look.title: Real or Invented?
look.text: A list of names from Fist of Fury: Huo Yuanjia, the teacher who has just died. The Jingwu school in Shanghai. Chen Zhen, the loyal student. The year, around 1910.
look.prompt: Sort the list into real and invented. Which item on the list is fictional, and how do you know?

check.q: Who is Chen Zhen?
choices: A fictional student invented for film
check.why: Chen Zhen was invented for Fist of Fury and returned in later films.

check.q: Where is Fist of Fury set?
check.why: The film takes place at the Jingwu school just after Huo's death in 1910.

check.q: What is true of a historical film?
choices: It must use only real events
It is always made by a government

check.why: Historical films mix real names and places with invented events.

lessons.title: Ip Man: Teacher and Film Hero
lessons.mainIdea: Ip Man was a real Wing Chun teacher in Foshan and Hong Kong; films since 2008 turned his life into a patriotic drama.
reading: Ip Man was born in Foshan, Guangdong, in 1893. He learned Wing Chun there. In 1949, as the Chinese Civil War ended, he moved to Hong Kong. In the early 1950s he began teaching Wing Chun to paying students. He taught there until his death in 1972.

Ip Man's students opened schools in many countries. His most famous student was Bruce Lee. Other students, such as his sons Ip Chun and Ip Ching, also taught widely. Many Wing Chun schools today trace their *lineage* through Ip Man.

In 2008, the film Ip Man came out, starring Donnie Yen. It shows Ip in Foshan during the Japanese occupation of the late 1930s and 1940s. Its most famous scenes are invented for drama. Sequels followed in 2010, 2015 and 2019. Their success brought many new students to Wing Chun schools.

The films present Ip as a *patriotic* hero who defends China's honor. School records present him as a teacher who ran classes and trained students. Both images are now part of how people remember him. Historians keep the two apart.

words.d: a line of teachers and students traced back through the generations
showing love and loyalty to one's country
a southern Chinese style from Guangdong, taught in Hong Kong by Ip Man

look.title: A Wall of Photographs
look.text: A Wing Chun school has a row of framed photographs on its wall. The first shows Ip Man in Hong Kong in the 1960s. Next come his student, that student's student and finally the current teacher. A small movie poster of Ip Man (2008) hangs by the door.
look.prompt: Which items on the wall record the school's lineage, and which record film history?

check.q: In which city was Ip Man born in 1893?
check.why: Ip Man was born in Foshan, Guangdong, and learned Wing Chun there.

check.q: When did Ip Man move to Hong Kong?
check.why: He moved to Hong Kong in 1949 and began teaching in the early 1950s.

check.q: Who starred in the 2008 film Ip Man?
check.why: Donnie Yen played Ip Man in the 2008 film and its sequels.

lessons.title: Origin Stories in School Names
lessons.mainIdea: Many style names honor founders from a school's own tradition, and historians label the stories behind them as tradition or legend when records are missing.
reading: Many Chinese style names contain a person's name. Hung Gar means Hung family. Its tradition honors Hung Hei-gun, a figure said to have learned at a southern Shaolin temple. Historians have not found records that confirm his life or that temple's story.

Wing Chun has a famous *origin story*. It says a Buddhist nun named Ng Mui taught a young woman named Yim Wing-chun, and the style took her name. Wing Chun schools tell this story with pride. Historians label it a legend, because no records from the time confirm it.

Choy Li Fut was founded, by its own tradition, by Chan Heung of Guangdong in 1836. By that tradition, its name honors two of Chan Heung's teachers, Choy Fook and Li Yau-san, and Fut, the Cantonese word for the Buddha. Here, the school's tradition gives a date and a founder. Outside records about him are few.

A school's *tradition* is what it teaches about its own past. Traditions carry meaning, honor teachers and build belonging. Historians report them respectfully. They also say clearly which parts are confirmed by records.

words.d: a story a group tells about how it began
what a group teaches and passes on about its own customs and past

look.title: Three Labels for One Story
look.text: A museum label about Wing Chun reads: 'According to Wing Chun tradition, the nun Ng Mui taught Yim Wing-chun, who gave the style its name. Historians have not found records from the time that confirm this story. Records of Wing Chun teachers in Foshan in the 1800s do exist.'
look.prompt: Which sentence reports a tradition, which reports a gap in the records, and which reports a record?

check.q: What does Hung Gar mean?
check.why: Gar means family; the style honors Hung Hei-gun from its tradition.

check.q: Why do historians label the Ng Mui story a legend?
choices: No records from the time confirm it
check.why: Wing Chun schools tell the story, but no records from the time confirm it.

check.q: What does the name Choy Li Fut honor, by its own tradition?
choices: Two of Chan Heung's teachers and the Buddha
check.why: By the school's tradition, Choy and Li are two of Chan Heung's teachers, and Fut is the Cantonese word for the Buddha.

lessons.title: Kung Fu on American Television
lessons.mainIdea: The TV series Kung Fu (1972–1975) spread the word to American homes, and its casting reflected Hollywood's long habit of giving Asian roles to white actors.
reading: Kung Fu was an American television series on the ABC network from 1972 to 1975. It told of Kwai Chang Caine, a half-Chinese man trained at the Shaolin Monastery. Caine wanders the American West in the 1800s. Each episode mixed a Western with flashbacks to his temple training.

The role of Caine went to David Carradine, a white American actor. For decades, Hollywood had often given Asian roles to white actors. This practice is called *yellowface* when makeup or costume is used to make a white actor look Asian. Asian American actors and groups criticized the practice. They said it kept them out of roles and spread a *stereotype* of Asian people.

The show's temple scenes came from the writers' imagination. They mixed real names, such as Shaolin, with invented lessons and sayings. For many American viewers, the show was their first picture of Chinese martial arts. That picture was a film set, not a real monastery.

Fans of Chinese arts and scholars have since pointed out what the series got wrong. Later films and shows cast more Asian and Asian American actors in leading roles. The debate over Kung Fu is now part of the history of how Americans learned the word.

words.d: the practice of using makeup or costume so a white actor can play an Asian character
a fixed, oversimplified idea about a group of people
choosing which actors play which roles

look.prompt: What would a historian want to check about this listing? Think about the temple, the story and the casting.

check.why: Kung Fu ran on the American network ABC.

check.q: What is yellowface?
choices: Makeup or costume used so a white actor can play an Asian character
check.why: Asian American actors criticized yellowface for keeping them out of roles.

choices: A film genre from Hong Kong

check.why: Critics said the show spread stereotypes about Chinese people and arts.

lessons.title: Karate in the Title, Kung Fu on Screen
lessons.mainIdea: The 2010 remake of The Karate Kid moved the story to Beijing and showed kung fu while keeping a title about karate, an Okinawan and Japanese art.
reading: The first Karate Kid film came out in 1984. It is set in Southern California. The actor Pat Morita played Mr. Miyagi, a teacher from Okinawa. Karate grew on Okinawa, once the Ryukyu Kingdom. So the film's title and its teacher matched.

In 2010, a remake of The Karate Kid came out. It starred Jaden Smith and Jackie Chan. The story moved to Beijing, China. Jackie Chan plays a maintenance man named Mr. Han, who teaches Chinese martial arts. Yet the English title still said karate.

Reviewers pointed out the mismatch at the time. Karate and Chinese arts come from different places and have different histories. The studio kept the famous title because audiences already knew it. A *brand* is a well-known name used to sell a product.

This case shows how names can travel apart from the things they name. A film title can follow what sells tickets. A school name follows its style, its place and its teachers. Careful readers ask which kind of name they are reading.

words.d: a new film made from the story of an older film
a well-known name used to sell a product
an island group, once the Ryukyu Kingdom and now part of Japan, where karate grew

look.prompt: How many years separate the first Karate Kid from its remake?

check.why: The remake moved the story to Beijing, China.

check.why: Karate grew on Okinawa; the 1984 film's Mr. Miyagi came from there.

check.q: Why did the studio keep the title The Karate Kid in 2010?

Audiences already knew the famous title
check.why: The title worked as a brand, even though the film showed Chinese arts.

lessons.title: Jeet Kune Do: Naming a New Art
lessons.mainIdea: In 1967 Bruce Lee gave his own approach a new name, Jeet Kune Do, showing that martial art names can be created by one person at one date.
reading: Bruce Lee opened schools in Seattle, in Oakland in 1964 and in Los Angeles in 1967. He called the early schools the Jun Fan Gung Fu Institute. Jun Fan was his Chinese name. His teaching began from Wing Chun but drew on many other arts.

In 1967, Lee chose a new name: *Jeet Kune Do*. In Cantonese it means the way of the intercepting fist. Unlike most older style names, this one has a known inventor and a known date. Lee also said he did not want it treated as a fixed style.

After Lee died in 1973, his students kept teaching. They disagreed about what the name should cover. Some kept a small, close group. Others taught more widely and mixed in other arts. Lee's family later formed an organization to protect his name and legacy.

Jeet Kune Do is a clear example of a *founder* naming an art. It stands beside Hung Gar and Wing Chun, whose founders are known through tradition. It also stands beside film names like the invented sects in wuxia novels. Each kind of name has its own kind of evidence.

words.d: the name Bruce Lee gave his approach in 1967; Cantonese for the way of the intercepting fist
the person who starts a school, style or organization

look.title: Three Kinds of Names
look.text: Name A: Jeet Kune Do, named by Bruce Lee in 1967. Name B: Wing Chun, named by tradition after Yim Wing-chun. Name C: a mountain sect in a wuxia novel, invented by the author.
look.prompt: What kind of evidence supports each name? Rank them from most documented to least.

check.why: Lee chose the name Jeet Kune Do in 1967.

check.q: What was the name of Lee's early schools?
